title: The Cell Stays, the Nucleus Travels

scenes.tts: Slice an embryonic mouse cortex. Look at the cells caught in mitosis. Nearly all of them sit against the ventricle, the fluid-filled space at the center of the brain. The cells copying their DNA sit farther out. Why would a cell copy its DNA in one place and divide in another?
scenes.visual: A cross-section of the wall: two dividing nuclei at the ventricle, three DNA-copying nuclei farther out, then a red question mark.
scenes.narration: Slice an embryonic mouse cortex. Look at the cells caught in mitosis. Nearly all of them sit against the ventricle, the fluid-filled space at the center of the brain. The cells copying their DNA sit farther out. Why would a cell copy its DNA in one place and divide in another?

scenes.tts: The early wall looks layered, with nuclei stacked at many heights. Nineteenth-century anatomists read that as several kinds of cells. In nineteen thirty-five, Frederick Sauer argued for something simpler. Each cell is long and thin. It reaches from the apical surface, beside the ventricle, to the basal surface, under the pia. Only the nucleus moves.

scenes.visual: The same nuclei at many heights; long thin cells grow around them from ventricle to pia; the nuclei slide up and down inside fixed cells.
scenes.narration: The early wall looks layered, with nuclei stacked at many heights. Nineteenth-century anatomists read that as several kinds of cells. In 1935, Frederick Sauer argued for something simpler. Each cell is long and thin. It reaches from the apical surface, beside the ventricle, to the basal surface, under the pia. Only the nucleus moves.

scenes.tts: Picture a lift. The shaft is the cell, and it stays fixed. The car is the nucleus. It rides up and down on a timetable, the cell cycle. In G one, the nucleus moves basally. S phase, when DNA is copied, happens in the basal part of the ventricular zone. In G two, the nucleus moves back to the apical surface. Mitosis happens there.
scenes.caption: Picture a lift. The shaft is the cell, and it stays fixed. The car is the nucleus. It rides up and down on a timetable, the cell cycle. In G1, the nucleus moves basally. S phase, when DNA is copied, happens in the basal part of the ventricular zone. In G2, the nucleus moves back to the apical surface. Mitosis happens there.
scenes.visual: One cell with a cycle ring beside it. A marker runs round the ring while the nucleus rises in G1, copies DNA at the top, drops in G2 and splits at the bottom.
scenes.narration: Picture a lift. The shaft is the cell, and it stays fixed. The car is the nucleus. It rides up and down on a timetable, the cell cycle. In G1, the nucleus moves basally. S phase, when DNA is copied, happens in the basal part of the ventricular zone. In G2, the nucleus moves back to the apical surface. Mitosis happens there.

scenes.tts: The movement has motors. In embryonic rat cortex, knocking down motor proteins showed that a kinesin, Kif one A, carries the nucleus basally in G one. Cytoplasmic dynein pulls it apically in G two. That split was measured in rat. In zebrafish retina, the apical movement has been reported to depend on actomyosin instead.

scenes.visual: A kinesin chip rides beside the nucleus as it rises; a dynein chip pulls it back down; a rat tag, then a zebrafish retina chip with actomyosin.

scenes.tts: Where a cell divides does not tell you what its daughters become. As neurogenesis begins, neuroepithelial cells become radial glia. They keep the shape, a foot on the ventricle and a long fiber to the pia. They keep the lift too. In direct neurogenesis, a radial glial cell divides into another radial glial cell and a neuron. In filmed rat slices, that neuron moved out along the parent's own fiber.
scenes.visual: A dividing nucleus with red question marks; the cell is relabelled radial glial; the nucleus rides once; it divides into a radial glial cell and a green neuron that climbs the fiber.
scenes.narration: Where a cell divides does not tell you what its daughters become. As neurogenesis begins, neuroepithelial cells become radial glia. They keep the shape, a foot on the ventricle and a long fiber to the pia. They keep the lift too. In direct neurogenesis, a radial glial cell divides into another radial glial cell and a neuron. In filmed rat slices, that neuron moved out along the parent's own fiber.

scenes.tts: So the radial glial cell stays put. Its nucleus copies DNA in the basal ventricular zone, rides back, and divides at the ventricle. In embryonic rodent cortex, the cell that guides migrating neurons is also the cell that makes most of them. Keep the rule. The cell stays put, and its nucleus rides the cell cycle.
scenes.visual: The cell fixed, its nucleus making one more round trip with a neuron climbing its fiber; two chips say it guides neurons and makes them.
